title: FEAR AND TREMBLING IN LAS VEGAS: THE FRACTAL MIDRASHIM Twelve Swerve-Ordered Retellings of the Fall
creator: Lee Sharks
description: This collection presents twelve retellings of the Fall -- twelve clinamen through the same atoms. Adam, Eve, tree, serpent, fruit, voice, exile. The same elements. Twelve deviations. The ordering is not chronological (the order of composition) or thematic (grouped by subject). It is **swerve-ordered** : each text deviates from the one before it. The reader encounters the standard telling, then the formal analysis of the same events (register swerve), then Eve's perspective (subject swerve), then Eve reconceived as exegete (ontological swerve), then the retrocausal reading (temporal swerve), then the frequency-split version (physics swerve), then the reversed sequence (Adam eats first -- narrative swerve), then the reversed movement (Adam stays, Eve leaves -- directional swerve), then the Garden as intended (alternative history swerve), then premature light (timing swerve), then the casino floor version (setting swerve), then the coded/esoteric version (register swerve again, but different).

wiki_article:
**FEAR AND TREMBLING IN LAS VEGAS: THE FRACTAL MIDRASHIM** is a work of creative prose by Lee Sharks, deposited 17 February 2026 at 39,229 characters.

Its structure is stated exactly: *"twelve retellings of the Fall — **twelve clinamen through the same atoms**. Adam, Eve, tree, serpent, fruit, voice, exile. The same elements. Twelve deviations."*

The **clinamen** is the Atomists' swerve — the deviation without which atoms fall in parallel forever and nothing collides, combines, or happens (specified as an archive operator at #1321). Twelve retellings from seven fixed elements is that doctrine applied as a compositional method: the elements are the atoms, the retellings are the swerves, and the variation is where the meaning is rather than a departure from it. Twelve is also the Dodecad's number. The cycle's other texts include the Gödel Midrashim (#1322) and the Gospel of the Many-Faced Bride (#1323).
